In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. These findings highlight the significance of incorporating linguistic structure inherent to pre-trained language models, which could lead to improved performance in various tasks requiring structural analysis. The code and data for this study are available at the following link: https://github.com/ghruvo/bart-word-order.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our system's versatility allows easy integration into popular deepfake detection datasets and platforms, enabling straightforward deployment in real-world settings. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghru/MD-CSDNetwork.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, the article also offers an answer to at least one additional problem that has been implicitly presented. Notably, the article's approach involves incorporating a key concept originally developed by the mathematician T. R. Hawkes. Moreover, the article demonstrates that the property of angle function can be re-expressed in terms of a set defined by inclusion and proximity, which allows for additional insight and also facilitates connections to other mathematical frameworks such as order theory and congruence distributive varieties. Finally, the article provides a proof that shows that the embedding of spaces with angle functions is actually equivalent to the embedding of the associated order structures, which in turn allows for the extension of its results to more complex varieties. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. Furthermore, we explore the stability of these relationships under field extensions and the effect of field extensions on the solitar invariants of curves. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Our data coverage spans from the launch of the scheme in April 2020 until the end of October 2021, a period during which the scheme distributed approximately $321 million in profits to its participants. Our study sheds light on the innovative ways Forsage promoters exploited linguistic ambiguities and cryptic blockchain transactions to operate below the radar of regulatory authorities, as well as the scheme's success in attracting a particular type of user referred to as "tokens only holders". Our research into the code and transactions of Forsage has significant implications for the detection of similar pyramid schemes built into smart contracts. Our approach to analyzing the scheme's promotional content on videos and social media provides a model for detecting deception in the investment information presented to users. Our study into the financial transactions of Forsage has a significant bearing on the theory of pyramid scams, as well as on the statistics of random binary trees, by offering a formula for the distribution of the length of these trees. Our research into the distribution of funds retained by Forsage participants provides a new understanding of the concept of income inequality. Our analysis of the scheme's code and transactions has a relevance to the broader context of the issues surrounding non-fungible tokens, as well as to the problems of preventing fraud in lotteries. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We have published the research in the form of a catalog featuring the basic properties of the 19 candidates evaluated in this study. We have also included 19 additional previously documented bulge cluster candidates based upon RR Lyrae star research, combining the two lists to create a comprehensive catalog of 38 candidate globular clusters within the galaxy's bulge. The research relied heavily on the infrared VVV survey data, particularly the K-band magnitude assessments, and the metal composition and ages were based upon comparisons with model stellar evolution, motion through space, and atmospheric composition, requiring further observation to confirm the findings. The proposed catalog candidates are located in the region of the galaxy accessible to the ATLAS project. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This indicates that even mild ribbons in longer wavelengths can contain extreme far-ultraviolet radiative signatures in massive stellar flares, with enough power to photoionize a planetary upper atmosphere, with implications for exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. This model can be a valuable tool for predicting the effects of large flares on planetary atmospheres and for assessing the validity of future exoplanetary biosignatures in the near-ultraviolet region. This research was conducted by using data from the IUE, which is archived at MAST, and combining it with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, which was conducted by using data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, combined with the CHIANTI plasma spectra package, and the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare data was also used in a previous study by Neupert et al. (2014).

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. This work's contribution sits at the intersection of clustering, influence estimation, and data-driven identification, and either alone or combined with other methods can provide valuable insights for experts in various fields. The research is open-sourced at https://github.com/PSL-SISTINE/InfluenceClustering.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Moreover, we discover that each dimension of the sparse code corresponds to a specific linguistic element, and by analyzing these codes, we can identify interesting patterns of language. All source code and datasets used in this study are publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN. For practical applications, we recommend using the text generation model obtained by training a sparse GAN with a simple scheduler, as it yields the best results based on our evaluations. This research was previously published in the proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Research in Computational Linguistics, Kyoto, Japan, November 2021. The results presented in this paper have been further improved and represent the baseline for our subsequent innovative approaches, such as sparse GAN models with internal critics and neural differential operators. We discovered that one of the dimensions of the sparse code is sensitive to style, which enables us to develop a simple and effective style transfer model by simply adding a corresponding sparse code as input to the decoder, without the need for any additional training. This research was previously published in the proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Computational Linguistics, Barcelona, Spain, August 2020. Moreover, we discovered that another dimension of the sparse code corresponds to an importance indicator, which enables us to develop a simple and efficient sampling strategy for text generation, as well as a score function for ranking generated sentences. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our research delivers capture-recapture models that can be used by itself to analyze resource selection, and new models that integrate capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate population density, space usage, and resource selection simultaneously.  We apply and evaluate these methods with real data to demonstrate their functionality.  Our findings highlight potential difficulties with using standard capture-recapture models on areas with complex habitat structures and recommend using capture-recapture models that account for space usage in such scenarios.  We also introduce two new measures of environmental variability that can be utilized by capture-recapture models and provide real data examples of these measures.  Our study and models can be utilized in various wildlife studies and management practices involving open populations living within complex habitat structures.  We discuss these models in conjunction with recent advances in static occupancy models, and highlight future research opportunities on models that integrate occupancy, capture-recapture, and resource selection data. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. From a practical perspective, it allows for the implementation of multilayer networks on existing numerical tools, enabling the visualization of solutions and the generation of multilayer Jacobian matrices. Our method is particularly useful for multilayer networks comprising multiple connected components. In such networks, the development of global synchronization patterns relies on the integration of isolated components and the connection between them. However, the analysis of these systems is challenging due to the presence of isolated components and the lack of a unified matrix representation. To address this limitation, we introduced an expanded joint matrix representation that includes dummy nodes in the isolated components. The inclusion of these nodes enables the use of the Kuramoto matrix approach in the analysis of these systems. Specifically, we used this method to examine the stability of the synchronized state in a ring configuration and a configuration featuring a looped connection. Additionally, we used a numerical method to investigate a random multilayer network comprising two layers. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the algorithm's size estimation is guaranteed by theoretical analysis, which establishes a lower bound on the accuracy of the estimate among the genuine nodes based on the number of genuine nodes that affirm the estimate and the number of malicious nodes that can confuse the algorithm. Our solution also includes a strategy for establishing a lower bound on the number of nodes that confirm the estimate, thereby providing a means to validate the accuracy of the algorithm's size estimation in real-world applications. The algorithm's precision was initially demonstrated through theoretical means and later verified through simulation experiments, which revealed that the algorithm's performance conforms to the predicted guidelines despite some variation among individual simulation outcomes. Our most spacious network tested, consisting of 10,000 nodes, exhibited a node density as low as 4/log(n), and the simulation validated the estimated precision of the algorithm's size estimation for all tested network densities, including densities greater than that particular scenario. Lastly, we investigated a novel approach to enhance the precision of the algorithm by increasing the network's density gradually and discovered that the algorithm's performance could be further improved. Our general conclusion is that uncertain networks possessing complex topology are amenable to efficient, precise size estimation through the introduction of temporary, gradual density increases. The most concise version of our algorithm requires the participation of nodes that consist of a single node that possesses complete knowledge of the network, which can be realized in a real-world setting by implementing the algorithm within a semi-decentralized manner in a network with a dense inner section. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. A specialized public code has been developed to showcase and expand this method, which can be used as a standalone solver or integrated into existing numerical relativity frameworks. A distinctive feature of this method is the straightforward recovery of physical quantities from the conformally decomposed components, achieving a precise match with standard approaches through adjustment of method parameters. As a result, this method can be used to explore scenarios involving fundamental fields in numerical relativity, paving the way for a wider range of simulations with a range of field types. A hallmark of this method is its compatibility with dynamic simulations, achieved by modifying the Hamiltonian constraint to express the conformal factor in terms of spatial derivatives, which leads to hyperbolic equations that arise through conformal rescaling of geometric quantities. A specialized application of this method to dynamic simulations involves replacing the source term in the Hamiltonian constraint with a delta-function surface density, which allows for the simulation of spinning down black holes, and similar scenarios involving matter distribution on a sphere. A comprehensive overview of the method, alongside illustrative pictures and algorithmic details, is provided in the form of a supplementary document available online. A distinguished aspect of this method is its uniqueness, which has been confirmed through an extensive analysis of the method's mathematical characteristics, alongside a comparison with standard approaches and alternative methods, such as the commonly used Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition, and the recently introduced Hyperboloidal Multidomain Multigrid solver. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We find that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a small value of approximately 1.1$\times 10^{-5}$ cm$^3$K$^{-1}$, and our results highlight the potential of this material to serve as a component in thermal to electrical energy harvesting and conversion technologies.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. We demonstrate this approach across scattering and spectroscopic measurements at the COHEREN, HiTES, and IDD beamlines at the NSLS-II. All code used in this study is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/NSLS-II/ML-at-NSLS-II. We invite users and developers to collaborate and contribute to this framework, embracing open-source principles to accelerate advancements in machine learning at user facilities. With this approach, researchers can focus on developing high-performance machine learning models while scientists and engineers at facilities concentrate on integrating these models into existing workflows, thereby expediting the path from data collection to insights. The approach presented here serves as a blueprint for similar user facilities, offering a foundation for interacting machine learning models that can be adapted to suit the needs of various beamlines and experiments. The development of a GUI tool called ML Opera enables users to create and customize machine learning pipelines for real-time use, facilitating interactions between beamline operators, users, and machine learning experts. The ML Opera interface is customizable, allowing users to modify the pipeline following the guidelines outlined in the NSLS-II Workflow and Data Management Policy, which stresses open standards, accessibility, and reproducibility. The tool also includes features for validating pipelines, monitoring pipeline performance, and identifying issues with experiments. The development of the ML Opera GUI was conducted in conjunction with the NSLS-II Operations and Machine Learning Groups. The code for ML Opera is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/NSLS-II-ML-Opera. We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles. Ultimately, this leads to constructing various specific G_K-invariants, ultimately enabling us to determine the 2-Selmer group structure and recover a subset of the original conjecture proposed by Serre. Moreover, we propose a simpler, more general proof of a result previously established by Diamond. Additionally, this approach reveals the isomorphism type of the 2-Selmer group for both odd and 2-prime number fields, provided certain condition is met. Lastly, we outline a strategy for expanding our methods to GL_2 cases involving Ramified fields. The proposed approach may also be compared to the method employed by Ennis. We establish a precise result for optimal solutions in an isoperimetric problem outside a confined object within the scenario where a large amount of space is considered, denoted as the 'large volume regime.' In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Alongside DECENNT, we introduce a more efficient mini-batch version of the ADI estimator and a multi-task learning DECENNT model, enabling decentralized data training and dynamic graph learning without access to extensive data. We thoroughly evaluate DECENNT and its variants across multiple metrics to demonstrate its effectiveness in various applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/yashsf/DECENNT.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The methodology has been applied to GPU acceleration of the Kronecker multi-resolution algorithm, a state-of-the-art method for logistic regression on large sparse matrices. The results show that the Nested Neumann method outperforms the Neumann Series and Newton iteration in most cases, exceeding the baseline performance by up to 10 times following appropriate tuning, and demonstrating scalable performance in GPU testing up to 4096 cores. The code for the Nested Neumann method has been released under the Apache Open Source License on GitHub. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Two theoretical models explaining radial and elliptic flow's development are used to interpret observations.  The Event Shape Engineering method's effectiveness is demonstrated by these results, yielding unique insights into initial state conditions and the angular momentum of the system.  Additionally found is that charged hadron distributions align with radial flow behavior predicted by four theoretical models, citing exponential decay constants of 4.09 GeV and 3.94 GeV for two models respectively, and 3.84 GeV for two other models where one has a slight centrality dependence of 3.82 GeV at 0-5\% and 3.86 GeV at 5-10\%.  Elliptic flow coefficient dependence on event-shape is well described by two models, exhibiting similar behavior and explaining observations with the same underlying physics.  Dependence on transverse momentum and centrality is investigated and reported.  Challenges are discussed involving transverse momentum dependence and possible solutions, such as using identified hadrons.  The study's outcomes are applicable to higher collision energies such as those for lead-lead collisions at a 5.02 TeV collision energy. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm provides greater flexibility in simulating flow dynamics with a wide range of particles, offering multiple time steps that can be further optimized for different components of flow simulations. Our code is available online for public use.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, this system's performance was tested under sudden ground changes and with different surface slopes. This research provides a method for efficiently simulating and optimizing ground reaction forces in a controlled environment, and the resulting force control system can be integrated with various terrain simulation models. Lastly, the development of this system highlights the limitations of the RFT model and the need for more sophisticated terrain simulation tools. This approach has been tested on a range of terrain scenarios, including hard ground, and the performance of the one-legged hopping robot meets industry standards. This work has significant implications for the development of legged robots capable of navigating complex environments. This research has been applied to optimize the robot's performance in various scenarios, including increasing its height, reducing foot size, and adding mass to the robot. This project provides a comprehensive Legged Robot Simulation Tool (LRST), which can be used to simulate and optimize a wide range of legged robots moving on various surfaces. This tool has been utilized to tackle specific challenges, such as minimizing the size of the robot's foot, and it has consistently delivered results in line with industrial standards. This research has further enhanced the LRST tool to meet the needs of industry partners, and it has successfully simulated a range of scenarios, including the movement of rolling robots, by incorporating the necessary equations into the simulation environment. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM generates hierarchies by identifying latent topics that correspond to specific network nodes, thereby ensuring the resulting models align with the original network structure. Moreover, we demonstrate HDTM's capability to handle massive datasets by analyzing Wikipedia's complete content, comprising over 6 million articles and 13 million links. The resulting model, with 720 ranked nodes, is capable of accurately classifying 85% of articles, and we show that HDTM's performance can be further optimized for real-world applications by incorporating semantic meanings of network labels. The HDTM framework serves as a foundation for future developments, and our available implementation allows for easy adaptation and experimentation by the research community. The underlying data, model code, and implementation are available for public use. The paper is categorized under the topics for Natural Language Processing from a Human Perspective, and the Web and Social Media. The paper has no relevance to the topics for Virtual Entities. The associated codes can be accessed at https://github.com/saleem/hdtm. The associated data can be accessed at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1T9sD9sG6DgB5MaYhL5C9T1T9sG6DgB5M. The paper ended with a discussion and four potential research directions, including but not limited to the following: the exploration of alternative sampling methods for the non-parametric topics, the integration of HDTM with existing navigation optimization algorithms, the development of a user-friendly interface for the generated hierarchies, and the investigation of methods for updating the models with the arrival of new data. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Despite the artificially generated nature of these simulations, the results hold significant value as they provide a concrete, quantifiable example of the quench-annealing duality, offering a qualitative or, in more extreme cases, a 10-fold speedup in solution-finding compared to standard quantum annealing algorithms. Nonetheless, it is essential to note that this study was conducted using a quantum annealer of relatively limited proportions, and future investigations are necessary to validate these findings for larger, more sophisticated instances of the exact cover problem. Nonetheless, the results presented in this paper hold significant implications for the assessment and validation of quantum annealing algorithms, particularly as they relate to the quench-annealing duality and its inherent temporal stability. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In addition, VSI-driven turbulence also depends on the characteristics of the disk system it resides within, requiring a comprehensive study that takes into account multiple factors, including its composition, geometric structure, and evolution over time. Given the complexity of such an analysis, our research utilizes a simplified model to better understand the key factors influencing VSI-driven turbulence and dust development, ultimately leading to a conservative estimate of particle settlement development in HL Tau-like systems. Based on this calculation, we expect particles with a micrometer size to develop within the outer regions of these systems, excluding the area immediately surrounding the central peak. In the inner regions of these systems, VSI-driven turbulence could lead to particle development, contributing to the presence of larger particle sizes. In a separate effort, we examined the relationship between VSI-driven turbulence and the formation of gaps and channels within protoplanetary disk systems, requiring further investigation. In the current state of research, dust development's impact on VSI is understood through the stabilization of shear velocity, but more comprehensive analyses are necessary to fully comprehend the complex dynamics at play in these systems. As such, we propose a future research agenda that includes a comprehensive study of protoplanetary disk systems, focusing on the various ways dust development affects the inherent instability and turbulence within these systems, and the resulting impact on their structure and formation. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. We have also demonstrated that this scenario can be applied to a particular class of manifolds where the scalar curvature is constant, and the dimension is low, without the requirement of boundedness. Furthermore, this result has an associated corollary regarding the finite-dimensional nature of the set of harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds, without the restriction of being defined over the reals. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. This may have implications for correcting zero points in parallax measurements derived from missions like Gaia. The effect of a changing PPN $\gamma$ on stellar parallax measurements also has a small impact, primarily due to the limited range of scanning angles in such missions, leading to a derivative that can be approximated as constant. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement error is likely minimal, under 0.1 microarcseconds, and may have implications for assessing the accuracy of parallax measurements derived from missions like Gaia. This factor could be further significant in missions with greater parallax measurement accuracy. Given its potential, we suggest increasing the precision of PPN $\gamma$ in future missions like Gaia. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. The knowledge retrieved as part of this approach is also found to be highly precise, with an average of 84% correct answers among the top-ranked knowledge entries. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Coarse-to-Careful.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectrum analysis remains incomplete and cannot fully account for the key processes involving these common comet molecules. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution. It also highlights instances where certain cations are preferentially created over others, which can be inferred from spectral features in the UV to visible range, and presents a simple neural network-based predictor to anticipate composite spectral patterns based on molecular properties, such as bond distances and energy levels. By analyzing the most significant oxygen-based cation spectra, this study finds that the most frequent compositions of cometary neutral gas are often distinguished by specific spectral features in the 550-5500 angstrom range, and therefore, more comprehensive spectral data in this range would significantly enhance our comprehension of cometary neutral gas compositions. This study's findings are relevant to ongoing and future comet research, including missions like the Europa Clipper, the JUICE mission, and the Comet Interceptor, as well as laboratory experiments that simulate cometary plasma and neutral gas compositions. This research is also an example of a broader approach that can be applied to other molecular species and environments, not just cometary environments. This study's results are in the form of an interactive web application that is available at [www.molcations.com/comets](http://www.molcations.com/comets). This research was supported by the NASA Planetary Science and Astrobiology Division.

A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  The findings support expanding access to mental health treatment for those within the criminal justice system.  The research also highlights the potential for using administrative data to assess the efficacy of court-ordered therapy and the potential tax benefits to institutions that provide such programs.  The results can be achieved through programs like the ones analyzed, which provided treatment worth approximately $1000 per year.  The most effective components of these programs are unknown, given the limited data available.  Possible opportunities for improving outcomes based on the data presented are also discussed.  The conventional methods used to assess the effect of mental health treatment also offer some novel extensions. Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. These results generalize previous work on the GMLE for the mean of a mixture distribution presented by Ghosh (1970). The chapter also includes an introduction to the method of mixing estimates proposed by Ghosh (1970) and its connection to GMLE. The chapter concludes with an discussion on the connection between the mixing estimation method and the method proposed by Le Cam (1973). The chapter ends with an discussion on the connection between the mixing estimation method and the method proposed by Le Cam (1973). Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. We also provide a brief discussion on real-world applicability and research directions in section 5 of the paper.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our optimal model achieved a 14% WER reduction on the NuSeD dataset. We also considered two other transfer methods: a bridge model and multi-task learning -- both yielded less impressive results. Nonetheless, our approach showed potential for other languages and we recommend it for further investigation. We're confident that our findings have significant implications for developing low-resource languages like Romani. Our code is available at https://github.com/thomashammer/czech_crf.

By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  Our research was granted the Best Paper Award at the 2022 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems.  Despite its success, this paper alone does not represent the findings of that conference. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/sentence-metadata-network.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, through our investigation, we also established that for any mechanism with any number of agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, the resulting allocations are fair up to one good with respect to their underlying values. Last but not least, we established that the two established methods have a key property called monotonicity, as well as showing that any mechanism with pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations or EFX allocations is not monotonic, thereby establishing a distinguished difference between them. Furthermore, we demonstrated that there exists an instance with three agents for the EF1 case, as well as a large class of instances with any number of agents for the EFX case, where the corresponding allocations are not fair. Finally, through our investigation, we established an upper bound on the number of pure Nash equilibria for a general instance with any number of agents, as well as proved that there exists a large class of instances with any number of agents, where the number of pure Nash equilibria is strictly less than this upper bound, thereby establishing a distinguished difference

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The anomalous behavior of its stars also supports the conclusion that UGC 8839 has experienced a significant gravitational interaction in the distant past. The observation of UGC 8839 is also significant because it underlines the importance of incorporating a distribution of initial rotation velocities when modeling galaxy evolution, and the phenomenon in UGC 8839 may have implications for understanding the evolution of low-mass spiral galaxies generally. The HII regions in UGC 8839 are the subject of a separate paper focusing on their physical characteristics. The data and analysis presented here have been made publicly available via the DOI link: 10.11570/46.741652. The research was funded by the National Science Foundation, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, the University of California, and the University of Colorado. The authors acknowledge the contributions of research associates and students whose work is recognized in the appendix. The paper is composed of nine sections including an introduction to UGC 8839, the analysis of its HII regions, the comparison with other galaxies, the dynamics of its disk, the stability of the HII regions, the distribution of luminosity, the interaction with a dwarf galaxy, the interaction with a giant galaxy, the implications for galaxy evolution, and the conclusion. The main text can be found in sections 2-8, with the analysis presented in the appendices. The HII region spectra are reported in appendix C, the extinction coefficients for the various ions are detailed in appendix D, the analysis of the gas velocity is presented in appendix E

Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Specifically, we test the validity of these predictions in situations where the quark mass approaches the mass of the threshold for breaking up a pion into two kaons. The results also shed light on the underlying physics of the I=2 pion amplitude system, which has been misunderstood until now. The mass range examined for the quarks spans from approximately 350 to 900 megaelectronvolts, covering both the quasi-continuum region and areas close to the threshold for producing two kaons. The investigation yields reliable physical outcomes even when the average quark mass is only lightly separated from the mass required to create two kaons. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-Education/SIT.

Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Consequently, single-particle entanglement cannot be considered as local context, as claimed by Gill and Massar. Consequently, even in the absence of entanglement, single-particle contextuality results in non-local effects, which can be optimized to enact context-dependent tasks. Finally, we propose an experiment that can detect single-particle contextuality and the associated non-local effects resulting from the spreading of the wave function during the measurement process, which is capable of being performed with today's technology. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Experimental results demonstrate accuracy of GMM-based codebooks and reliable performance in real scenarios, also showing the proposed method's versatility in adapting to changing channels.
