Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate the potential of TextWorldExpress, we established a record for the lowest possible solution time for a complex text-based adventure game, breaking the previous mark by more than a factor of ten. 
TextWorldExpress is open-source and compatible with multiple text-based game challenges, offering developers a versatile platform to accelerate a broad range of text-based games not just limited to those in the Express collection. 
For researchers and the virtual agent community, we created a simplified version of the original text-based games that can run on much older hardware, serving as a standard against which future optimizations can be measured. 
In a age where virtual agents are being integrated into increasingly sophisticated platforms, the importance of processing speed in text-based games has taken on a new level of urgency, making TextWorldExpress a vital tool that can help uncover and address various performance-related issues. 

Thanks to the contributions from multiple researchers, TextWorldExpress was made possible by the widespread availability of usable code. 
Specifically, it is derived from the following sources:

* Zombie Apocalypse: a text-based game challenge that is part of the TextWorld-DomainAdventures collection, available under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.
* One Room: another text-based game challenge found in the same repository, also under the same license terms.
* School Safety: the third text-based game challenge derived from the same source, once more licensed identically.
* The EasyClassic framework: a tool for creating and managing text-based games that is compatible with Google Colab and other similar platforms. 
* The TextWorldExpress domain: a domain that can be accessed at express.textgamelab.com. 
* The related GitHub repository: a repository that can be found at github.com/textgamelab/TextWorldExpress. 
* The related Google Colab notebook: a notebook that can be run from the colab.textgamelab.com website

The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The model and results also highlight the significance of examining intra-day dynamics and the potential side effects of redispatch and imbalance management on markets, as well as the necessity for robust methodological tools to evaluate and design ancillary services and electricity markets. The model is available online at https://github.com/ancillaryservices/acquisition_model.

A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The dissolution of the northern vortex typically begins in the fall, but it was notable that it started breaking apart in the summer, a phenomenon that has not been observed before. The remaining debris from the vortex was seen as far as 65 degrees latitude and took several years to clear out of the area. The extensive data collected from the Cassini spacecraft have enabled a comprehensive analysis of the northern vortex's formation, dissolution, and seasonal variability. The findings from this study can be applied to other polar terrestrials, such as Mars and Venus, and have implications for the understanding of atmospheric waves and their effects on temperature and chemistry in these environments. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. The novel algorithm developed here here can also find use in other two-dimensional experiments that involve scattering or autocorrelation. The risk of noise accumulation over time, a challenge in many retrieval applications, is addressed by a new time-domain implementation of the algorithm that significantly minimizes noise, a level that cannot be achieved with other methods. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. The development of our method, the associated code, and extensive test case results are made freely available to the public. The underlying approach is applicable to various real-world scenarios such as geo mechanical applications and subsurface flow analysis. The code is implemented using the Dune suite of finite element tools and the C++ programming language. The project was conducted under the support of the German Research Foundation (DFG). Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. This study provides a freely accessible toolkit for the cognitive science community, consisting of RStudio documents, R scripts, and the sampling algorithm implemented in C++ that can be used to validate Bayes factor estimates and ensure their accuracy and reliability. This approach can be applied to various research scenarios, including the evaluation of structural theories, the investigation of individual data, and the comparison of different models, with the possibility of extending it to other research areas beyond cognitive science. Along with the C++ sampling algorithm and R scripts, this research includes a concise version of the code that can be used for replication purposes. This research received no external funding. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Experimental evaluations have validated the accuracy of DiscSense, and the findings are expected to contribute to the development of rigorous standards for the classification of English discourse indicators. Furthermore, DiscSense is available at https://github.com/TharunChandru/DiscSense.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our pre-trained models and data are available for download at: \url{https://github.com/ghrua/MCSEC}.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. This limitation is also reflected in the model's results, which show that introduced variables representing refugee populations and their connections to the wider community significantly influence the model's predictions of rioting distribution and mobility patterns. Notably, these results align with local accounts of the riots' impact being most severely felt in outer Santiago. Furthermore, the model facilitates understanding of how disturbances in outer regions can escalate into capital city riots, consistent with first-hand reports from protesters. This model's limitations provide valuable insights for potential improvements, including the integration of elements reflecting population displacement, outer neighborhood dynamics, and the effects of protests in the capital city. This has implications for modeling similar large-scale disturbances in capital cities with defined neighborhoods. Failing to account for population displacement and the distinct dynamics of the capital city may lead to biased or incomplete interpretations of model results. This research involves collaborating with local experts to integrate additional data, including public transportation usage and demographic information about Santiago's neighborhoods. This collaboration also involves assessing the theoretical effects of different transmission and migration parameters on model outcomes, with the goal of further improving the model's effectiveness in predicting rioting dynamics. This research presents a novel approach to modeling the riots' spatial distribution using an epidemiological non-local approach, with results suggesting that this method can accurately capture the temporal progression of riots but requires refinement to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. This research provides a starting point for further model development, with potential applications to analyzing the spread of other phenomena in complex networks, including epidemiological outbreaks, traffic dynamics, and social movements in capital cities. This model can be adapted to analyze the temporal progression of riots with similar dynamics but struggles to capture the distribution of unrest in a new location without adequate data and proper parameter tuning. This research involves making the model's source code publicly available on GitHub, along with instructions for using it to simulate the 2019 Chilean riots. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. We also explore the application of our method to regular expressions over finite sets of characters, showing that our approach in such cases outperforms traditional methods in terms of computational efficiency. Moreover, we investigate the potential for our algorithm to extract meaningful statistics from the solving process, demonstrating that it is possible to extract insights about the containment issue by analyzing the tree structure of the solving process. We have implemented our method in a proof-of-concept solver called DeepRegEx, making it available for public use. Alongside this implementation, we present a collection of challenging inequality instances solved using DeepRegEx, offering a benchmark for evaluating the performance of containment solving algorithms. We also explore the relationship between containment and the intersection of regular languages, presenting a decision-making procedure for this problem and showing that it is computationally intractable. Finally, we outline a path for extending our method to other types of regular language inequalities. The development of DeepRegEx and the underlying solving method mentioned above were both achieved through an automated process, using a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. The proposed method's superiority is also proven by evaluating the model on datasets with both smooth and rapid movement. The code is available at: https://github.com/yangkgg/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Both theoretical and experimental findings can be generalized to higher-order semimetals, suggesting that 3D solid-state systems enriched with diverse nonlinear Weyl semimetal properties await discovery.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. A comparative analysis is also presented, highlighting the impact of different regularization techniques and mesh refinement on the solution and error analysis. A particular application to electromagnetic tomography is described. The study relies on the presence of a thin layer around the inaccessible boundary where the electric field and its derivative are known, a setting that is analogous to that found in actual scenarios. A note on the method's potential extension to the static case and the necessity of imposing additional constraints to obtain smooth solutions are included in the appendix. A brief overview of the method and the analysis is provided in the conclusion, along with some thoughts on future improvements and possible adaptations to actual experimentation setups. The study's findings are reflected in the numerical results graphed in the figures and the algorithmic approach to solving the problem is detailed in the pseudocodes presented in the text. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. The resulting code is now available online, awaiting the contribution of model data from various sources that can demonstrate the limitless potential of FedSA.

A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition, is used to measure the change in a region's entanglement entropy along a null direction in order to understand the quantum thermodynamics of complex systems. Investigating whether the quantum null energy condition limits irreversible entropy generation during quenching driven by an influx of energy and momentum from an infinite, memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories, our research finds that an increase in both entropy and temperature, as required by the classical Clausius inequality, is necessary to prevent a violation of the quantum null energy condition, specifically in quenching transitions that result in changes in thermal states dual to Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli geometries. Additionally, our research provides lower and upper bounds for the change in entropy or temperature for a specific change in temperature or entropy in any initial state. Furthermore, our results indicate that the null energy condition is never overstepped in time and that the asymptotic rates can be determined analytically. Our study demonstrates that the entanglement entropy within a region of a specific length, $l$, eventually reaches a steady-state within a time frame of $l/2$ with an exponential decay rate of $3/2$, and that the coefficient for the quadratic growth of entanglement in time can be found for any $l$, and that the asymptotic rate of growth for a semi-infinite interval is directly proportional to the difference of the entropy densities of the initial and final states, along with determining the upper and lower limits for these rates of growth. We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. This research also leads to an investigation of the relationship between different measures of asymmetry, including a proposal for a new monotonically increasing function called the quadratic standard deviation, whose simplest form is directly related to the well-known Vaidella-Virniati (VV) convex roof measure of asymmetry. As a result, we are able to establish several important facts about the VV measure, such as its connection to the quadratic system-environment entanglement, the characterisation of its non-negativity, and the proof that it is equivalent to the worst case scenario of system-environment scattering, as well as the relation to the Bhatia, Davis, and Goldstein (BDG) matrix norm, whose combination yields the quadratic speed limit equation. Furthermore, this investigation enables us to explore the relationship between the VV measure and the BDG matrix norm, which leads to the conclusion that the quadratic speed limit equation holds when the initial state condition is set to the worst case scenario, namely the maximum VV measure. This research on the quantum speed limit also considers the case of time-dependent Hamiltonians, for which we derive an expression for the time-averaged asymptotic distance, as well as the case of a specific Hamiltonian error, for which we derive an expression for the time-averaged asymptotic distance. Finally, we investigate the relationship between the VV measure and the quadratic system-environment entanglement, as well as the average thermal state, for which we derive an expression for the time-averaged asymptotic distance. This investigation leads to an understanding of the quantum speed limit equation, as well as the time-averaged asymptotic distance, as well as the average thermal state, for which we investigate the conditions under which the quantum speed limit equation is satisfied,

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This study highlights the potential of integrated quantum elements, combining multiple materials, to serve as quantitative proxies for research on material flaws causing decoherence. This terahertz approach can be expanded to examine other quantum systems, such as Josephson junctions and ferroelectric quantum circuits. This research was conducted at the NHMFL at Florida State University.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is tailored to contribute to the ongoing discussion within the scientific community and to guide future research and potential missions to study the planet's interior, surface, and atmosphere, as well as its complex interactions and how they have shaped the planet's evolution and its implications for Earth. Understanding Venus's evolution also provides valuable insights for searching for similar processes on other planets and exoplanets. The work includes extensive appendices that provide additional information on atmospheric escape, atmospheric chemistry, and spectroscopic observations. The paper for the most part is written at an advanced level but with clear summaries of the complex processes and scenarios discussed. The target audience is the scientific community specifically in the fields of planetary science, geology, astronomy, and chemistry but it may also be accessible to graduate level students in these fields. The work is organized into seven sections with an extensive abstract provided at the beginning and brief summaries at the end of each section. The sections address the sources of volatiles, the interactions with the core and mantle, the interactions with the surface, the interactions with the upper atmosphere, the escape from the atmosphere, the feedback cycles, and the evolution scenarios. The paper includes seven figures and four tables but the figures and tables are primarily straightforward and do not require a deep understanding of the complex processes and scenarios discussed. The paper concludes with six figures

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. If the input laser pulse contains a significant amount of elliptical polarization, the waveplate can maintain this inherent property while still increasing the peak power of the dominant component, which has also been demonstrated numerically. This indicates that the plasma waveplate is a highly versatile component that can be applied in a wide range of situations, as shown in a simulation where it successfully enhanced the peak power of a laser pulse to 5 PW. The interaction of the laser pulse with the plasma waveplate was also analyzed in another simulation where the plasma waveplate was changed to show that the conversion of linear to circular polarization is an inherent property of the specific waveplate designed, which can still increase the peak power of an elliptically polarized laser pulse to 4.8 PW. This type of plasma waveplate offers a promising solution for the efficient deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems, as shown in a final simulation where it successfully converted a 4.2 PW linearly polarized laser pulse to a 4.8 PW circularly polarized pulse. Re-examining the search for a nonzero electric dipole moment (EDM) form factor, $d_\tau(s)$, in $\tau^+\tau^-$ production via $e^+ e^-$ collisions between the $\tau$-pair threshold and $\sqrt{s} \sim 15$ GeV is considered. The optimal approach for sensitive $CP$-odd observables is explored, focusing on the real and imaginary parts of $d_\tau(s)$. The expected outcomes for optimal $CP$ observables in $\tau$-pair production at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV with $\tau^\pm$ decaying into leptonic or semihadronic modes are calculated, accounting for full kinematic information. For the Belle II experiment at the KEKB accelerator, with an integrated luminosity of 50 ab$^{-1}$ and assuming acceptance cuts, the achievable sensitivities for $d_\tau$ are estimated to be $6.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $4.0 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm for semihadronic decays, respectively. In the ideal case without particle cuts, the achievable sensitivities with $50$ ab$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV, corresponding to $4.5 \times 10^{10}$ $\tau^+ \tau^-$ events, would be $5.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $3.2 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm, respectively. Additionally, the magnitude of the $\tau$ EDM form factor in the type-II two-Higgs doublet and scalar leptoquark extensions of the Standard Model is investigated. The results show that the $\tau$ EDM form factor is generally the smallest among $\tau$, $K$, and barion EDMs but can exceed the achievable sensitivity at Belle II or reach the absolute stability limit in the scalar leptoquark model. The importance of incorporating the $CP$-odd observables related to the $\tau$-pair invariant mass in experimental analyses is also emphasized. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. In contrast, a random error model is considered, where the decoding of rank metric codes is guaranteed to successfully decode errors of up to n-k rank with a probability of at least 1 - p^n. For maximum rank errors, we derive a corresponding coverage probability of at least 1 - p^k. Both of these guarantees are achieved at the cost of transmitting k additional code symbols. In a third scenario, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error matrix, even those of maximal rank n. The development of these decoding strategies also enables the computation of rank metric code rates, specifically the rate at which errors of up to n-k rank occur, which is given by the formula (n-k)(k+1)/n. This expression can be applied to a variety of code constructions, including Gabidulin codes, the family known as TSD codes, and a new diverse class of rank metric codes, all with rates less than half. Finally, the development of a systematic approach to designing rank metric codes with symmetrical error behavior provides an additional contribution to the field. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Nonetheless, SN~2020jfo exploded with a high energy explosion mechanism similar to other SNe~II, and with a low mass loss rate, which may be attributed to its distant galactic host. Based on its explosive energy and low mass loss rate, we propose that SN~2020jfo's progenitor was a massive giant with a sub-solar metallicity. Nonetheless, more accurate measurements are necessary to confirm these findings. Moreover, the overlap of its nebular-phase [Fe~II] line strength with those of SNe~II and II-P, along with its relatively faint absolute peak magnitude, categorize SN~2020jfo as a hybrid Type II supernova. Nonetheless, SN~2020jfo's behaviour lasted for a shorter period than typical SNe~II-P, which may indicate that most SNe~II-P with similar absolute peak magnitudes have been misclassified, or other factors are at play, such as different hydrogen envelope masses, or various metallicity levels. Nonetheless, we conclude that SN~2020jfo exhibits unique characteristics, with a short plateau duration, low luminosity, and a distinct nebular-phase spectrum, making it an intriguing addition to the diverse range of Type II supernovae. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The proposed MuLE design consisting of 9 segments can also successfully detect a signal with a flux of ~10^-11 erg cm^-2 s^-1 within a 5 degree angular resolution. The MuLE concept can be applied to various applications, including  0.1-10 keV X-ray monitoring using LE mirrors with different aperture angles, and  wide-field soft X-ray monitoring using LE mirrors with a 10 arcmin field-of-view. The proposed MuLE design consisting of 9 segments can also be applied to  wide-field soft X-ray monitoring of transients in molecular clouds. The proposed MuLE design consisting of 9 segments has an optical efficiency of 2.8%, and the signal-to-noise ratio of the detected signal is 10 times greater than the optimal threshold for detecting an X-ray transient, which forms the basic requirements for the wide-field soft X-ray monitoring of transients in molecular clouds. The proposed MuLE design consisting of 9 segments can be realized through a combination of 2D LE mirrors and a 3D mirror arrangement, and the segmentation of the LE mirror can be achieved using a variety of methods including mechanical cutting, electroforming, and 3D printing. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. 

These models have been compared to established theories and numerical solutions, with results showing they yield identical answers when conditions are highly simplified, and demonstrating the accuracy of our method in both static and dynamic scenarios. 

This new formulation has been applied to massive rotating stars with masses up to 20 solar masses, and has revealed novel insights about their composition, as well as determining key factors that influence their stability and behavior. 

Finally, this method has been designed to be suitable for a wide range of stellar evolution problems, and can be refined further to handle more complex scenarios.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We discuss the network's potential to enhance detection efficiency and provide theoretical groundwork for an improved design. Furthermore, the convolutional neural network's ability to recover known events holds value in its own right, given the limited number of detected neutron star and binary neutron star events. We have made the code available publicly to facilitate future improvements and discoveries. The deep learning approach has significant implications for future real-time detections of neutron star and black hole mergers involving compact binaries, and demonstrates the effectiveness of deep learning in the context of multi-messenger astronomy. We have realized all this with the humble starting point of just four detected neutron star and binary neutron star events. The immense potential of this technique, coupled with future detections, has the power to revolutionize our comprehension of dense matter. The ongoing LIGO and Virgo search for merging compact binaries in the 24-2500 Hz band offers ample opportunities for future analyses and discoveries. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. Moreover, this study highlights the significance of studying pure behavioral changes and their lasting effects on urban diversity, along with the financial implications for individuals and businesses. Lastly, this work provides a framework for assessing the long-term impact of reduced interaction due to the pandemic, which can be applied to other contexts beyond urban diversity, such as the impact on tourism or cultural events. Finally, by analyzing the declining willingness to visit new places, this research sets the ground for investigating underlying factors like changed preferences, economic influences, and business responses that may influence diversity of urban encounters in the long term. The underlying methodology and theoretical framework can also be applied to study the impact of other reducing factors on urban diversity, such as traffic restrictions or cultural policy changes. The data and analysis used in this research are available online at https://github.com/ghassab/Urban-Diversity.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Further testing on a larger campus with multiple layers, using up to five sonar sensors in real-time 3D navigation, is also shown. This method is suitable for wide-range navigation in diverse indoor environments, with diverse sonar sensor configurations possible. A comparative analysis with a mono-layer controller is also provided, offering insight into the layered control framework's performance. The developed system, combined with the sonar flow model and controller structure, has been made available online for further development and modification by the research community. The system's practical application has significant potential in various indoor navigation scenarios, such as in museums, offices, and large sporting stadiums. The development of the system also provides a platform for further innovation, with potential in areas like bio-engineering and astro-navigation. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture, specifically the limitations of large pre-trained language models like BERT, as well as the untapped potential of a wide range of applications such as question answering and machine translation. The study concludes by highlighting the curvatures' impact on a system's temporal stability, coupled with its geometric and stochastic properties, and emphasizing the necessity for further investigations into the curvatures' impact on random field models. When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance. Although the development of a guaranteed convergence optimization algorithm for general L1-PCA has been challenging and previously unachievable, this study provides a significant breakthrough in this area. The development of this algorithm also involves examining specific cases of its general form, one of which was previously uninvestigated, while the other case led to the discovery of a new majorizer with constant scaling factors for the absolute convergence criterion. The implementation of this algorithm for anonymous data collection is also presented. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. To validate our findings, we employ a mix of game-based evaluation methods and compare the annotated EMO20Q data sets against outcomes obtained using BERT-based annotation assistance. Lastly, we discuss potential applications and limitations of this approach to annotated data sets. As an example, we show that revising the annotations of EMO20Q yields a 7.4% improvement in classification accuracy. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This demonstrates the capabilities of atomic interferometry in detecting weak magnetic fields in the immediate environment of a superconductor, thereby enabling the characterization of superconducting materials, as well as providing a reliable approach for implementing magnetic field sensitivity near quantum computing components. Additionally, this principle can be applied to measure local electric field changes in superconductors, offering a means to evaluate position-dependent potential fluctuations, while also providing a means to detect near-surface material defects, such as surface imperfections and chemical dopants, that could affect the reliability of quantum operations. Moreover, this approach can be expanded to measure environmental effects on a macroscopic level, including the expelled fields from multiple superconducting components in a combined device, or the interaction between components and surrounding materials in devices, enabling the development of, for example, a quantum accuracy standard for superconductor-material interactions. While this concept can be applied across a wide range of combined systems, it is particularly well-suited for evaluating a particular important case: the interaction between atomic qubits and superconducting coexisting materials. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  We openly provide the DynaSOAr framework under an permissive BSD license to facilitate easy adoption across a range of object-oriented GPU applications.  Our framework source code is available at https://github.com/abhinavk91/DynaSOAr.  We also present a range of ready-to-use GPU examples at https://github.com/abhinavk91/DynaSOAr-Examples.  Our benchmark results indicate that DynaSOAr offers significant performance gains of up to 3 times for certain integer-based SIMD applications, as well as efficient memory usage and low fragmentation in both fully and partially parallelized scenarios.  Furthermore, our analysis reveals that DynaSOAr's speedup and memory efficiency gains primarily result from the reduced memory usage and lower average object sizes in particular cases, where the challenge of achieving suitable object sizing is a major obstacle for many GPU developers.  To address this issue, we created the DynaSOAr Size Advisor, a simple yet effective tool that recommends optimal object sizing for a given application, resulting in additional performance gains and easier GPU development.  Our research and findings have implications for a broader range of object-oriented GPU applications, and we openly provide the DynaSOAr

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. This theoretical model highlights the importance of proper magnetic alignment and orientation of the YSR states in comparison with experimental data. Moreover, it emphasizes the critical role of orbital decomposition in understanding YSR state behavior and analyzing local states along the d-axis, which cannot be achieved through other analysis methods. Lastly, this framework's capabilities in describing complex magnetic configurations and varying exchange fields make it a valuable tool for further research and comparison with experimental data.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. Although follow-up spectroscopy showed that TOI-712 is an active star with a slightly uncertain mass and radius, the team calculated the planetary masses as roughly $20 times that of Earth", and the surface temperatures of TOI-712 b and TOI-712 c to be about $362$ and $280" Kelvin respectively. The team also observed the planetary periods to be stable, and found evidence of two planetary phases: partial eclipses of one planet by another, and transits of one planet across the other's light, which could be common in exosystems. Further studies into this system are necessary, but it offers valuable insights into the formation of planetary systems and potential life-harboring planets on the outer reaches.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Lastly, our findings also highlight the necessity for accurate supercell sizing in order to obtain reliable results, as an under-sized supercell led to errors including anti-ferromagnetic ordering and N-O bonding.

We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Additionally, we introduce a new, more complex structure called the "pancake graph" and determine its associated $\lambda$ value. The development of our lower bound value relies on a more advanced "density testing" technique. The paper also discusses possible variations of the $\lambda$ value for other graph structures like cliques and odd cycles. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications. The theoretical understanding of this phenomenon is supported by three separate simulation approaches, each drawing from the principles of quantum electrodynamics in the context of strong-field physics. The efficiency of this positron polarization process is quite remarkable, with the potential to surpass the effectiveness of traditional methods used in scientific research and various technological systems. The findings of this research are likely to influence the design of future experiments aimed at optimizing the production of polarized electrons and positrons, primarily using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with a wide range of potential uses. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, it demonstrates that groups with a polynomial diameter are soluble if they have a relatively small number of conjugacy classes. This study also presents examples and counterexamples to illustrate the proposed criteria's requirements and the groups to which it applies. The proposed approach to measuring diameter allows for a significant extension of an earlier result by Tointon, which is previously established as a corollary. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. Furthermore, the temperature sensor's robustness was demonstrated in a real-world application, where it accurately monitored the temperature of a sub-threshold circuit while operating at a lower supply voltage. The proposed temperature sensor has been patented as part of the project's activities at the EU's Framework Program and the Spanish CENIT programs. The design has also been made available to industry partners for possible collaboration. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  Such investigation will be crucial in clarifying the degree to which the core mass function influences the resulting star formation mass function, with implications reaching to cloud scale star formation regulation.  This study's findings also appear to be specific to the Dragon cloud, as similar research within the Taurus complex does not reveal the same core mass growth among its cores.  The theoretical framework underlying this study is primarily based on the core mass function and the mass function of the associated outflows, using data from the Dragon cloud and drawing comparisons with data from the Taurus complex.  Specifically, the research involves using a Bayesian approach and Monte Carlo methods to analyze the core mass function and outflow mass function, with the outcome being a statistical representation of the outflow mass function in relation to the core mass function.  This statistical representation in turn enables the calculation of essential parameters such as the mass credibility exponent and the mass credibility coefficient for both the Dragon cloud and the Taurus complex. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. This relationship enables accurate prediction of the transition between these regimes, completing our understanding of the stick-slip to stationary transition in dry liquid foams. The findings of our study are relevant to a broader context involving the flow of complex liquids on various surfaces and may be applied to other non-Newtonian liquids beyond dry liquid foams. The importance of surface roughness in contributing to friction is also analogous to the role of contact angles in determining whether liquids form interfaces or films. The degree of surface roughness required to force the formation of interfaces rather than films or slippage has been demonstrated both visually and through stress measurements, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon. The research presented here may also contribute to the better design of surfaces for various applications involving the flow of complex liquids, including medical devices and equipment used in food processing. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes may be prevented by increasing the roughness of surfaces, forcing the formation of interfaces rather than slippage or films, and thus ensuring continuous and safe operation of such equipment. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. The data and code used in this report are available for public use.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghrua/look-ahead-attention.

Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. Just as grid computing provides a foundation to build upon, artificial intelligence can build upon the foundations of grid computing. We also explore the relationship between grid computing and artificial intelligence, noting that artificial intelligence represents a more comprehensive and richer field of study that includes grid computing as a subset.
