Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this methodology enables researchers to focus on developing better binary mask prediction models, which is a more accessible goal. To further enhance performance, this model is combined with eight state-of-the-art data augmentation techniques. Experimental evaluations conducted on three separate datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this model, which has also been applied to real-world cancer diagnosis tasks. Moreover, this model has been incorporated into a feature extraction module for a famous deep learning-based point annotation network, which has yielded a 6.8% absolute reduction in evaluation metrics. All models have been implemented using the PyTorch deep learning framework, which is available for public use. The code, alongside additional information about the W-Net model and the conducted experiments, has been provided on a public repository at https://github.com/ghruan/W-Net.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Finally, a validation of our findings through GCNN-based classification on multiple datasets shows the practical effectiveness of this approach. By breaking down the intricacies of GCNNs, we provide a concise and accessible explanation of these complex networks, offering a foundation for further innovation and improvement. A related Python code can be found at https://github.com/ghoul333/Matched_Ffilter_GCNN. A mathematical appendix is available in the paper files.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Specifically, the results indicate a 13 dB boost in the signal-to-noise ratio of lateral displacement estimates derived from VSSA in comparison to conventional SA, as well as a 50 Hz increase in the sampling frequency of VSSA. This research demonstrates the potential of VSSA in elastography, offering a straightforward and cost-effective solution to enhance imaging without the need for hardware modifications. The proposed technique provides actionable insights for developers and researchers aiming to advance elastography using SA and similar techniques. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our research highlights the challenges and opportunities in multi-task
reinforcement learning settings and showcases a number of promising techniques
for improving performance in such scenarios. Moreover, we show that simple forms
of network isolation can be highly effective and provide a comprehensive dataset
for future theoretical analyses. Last but not least, we open-source our code so
other researchers can build upon our findings.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. By combining these results, we derive several notable consequences and generalizations, including an undecidability result for certain formal systems and an unprovability statement for a specific arithmetic formula. This study's aim is to reveal the common underlying principles and patterns, and to demonstrate the closeness between these seminal results and their general form, with the ultimate goal of providing a platform for further exploration and extension beyond the original proofs. We invite mathematicians to explore this topic and its connections to other significant results, such as the Second Godel Incompleteness Theorem, the Godel-Carnap formula, and the decisional character of certain formal systems.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Our method's strong performance was also matched by the results of human evaluators in evaluation studies. Our code is available at https://github.com/shimothy/CGAN-posterior-sampling.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. The contribution of this current work extends that of a preceding study, from which it differs by incorporating novel approaches to invariant configuration specification. We also derive novel conditions for the preservation of quadratic surfaces in fractional-order systems. The article concludes with an exploration of the relationship between invariant surfaces and the number of system dimensions. The appendices provide supplementary mathematical proof and a numerical example illustrating the application of the proposed method to a specific fractional-order system. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Furthermore, this paper presents a detailed characterization of this particular screen, which could be observed directly during a planned direct imaging mission of the Local Bubble. The velocity of the screen was found to be similar to the velocity of the nearby interstellar medium, which is likely associated with the Local Bubble's movement. The detection of this screen also confirms the accuracy of previous estimates of the distance to the Local Bubble. The analysis of screen orientations in the line of sight to the pulsar B1133+16 revealed an misalignment of approximately 20 degrees between the normal to the screen and the line connecting the pulsar and the screen's center. The movement of the screen was found to cause changes in scintillation patterns on a timescale of one year, which could be important for future observations of this screen and similar screens in the line of sight to other pulsars. The data from the observations were used to create a detailed model of the scintillation patterns in the line of sight to the pulsar B1133+16, which could be useful for a planned direct imaging mission of the Local Bubble. The discovery of a screen associated with a localized void in the Local Bubble provides valuable information about the structure and morphology of this region of the interstellar medium. The analysis of the data from the observations also used a new method of analyzing scintillation patterns, which is more efficient than previous methods. The timescales of changes in scintillation patterns on either side of the beam formed by the Earth's motion around the Sun were found to be symmetrical, which is consistent with the effects of the beam of the pulsar. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Human evaluator ratings reveal that the proposed method exceeds the baseline WN model in terms of quality and pitch accuracy for unseen frequency inputs. Moreover, QPNet exceeds the state-of-the-art tacitly frequency-control DPCNN-based model, SpeechFormer, in terms of quality and pitch accuracy for unseen frequency inputs. The proposed model also generates a sentence synthesis example and a music demonstration to illustrate its versatility. The code for QPNet is available at the following repository: https://github.com/Chengwei601/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet. The proposed model's potential applications include but are not limited to text-to-speech, music generation, and modeling of other quasi-periodic signals. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/zhoukui, along with the VGG-Sound Source dataset accessible at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/data/vggsound_source.html.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. This inverse problem is ill-posed, and we address it by minimizing a cost function consisting of a least squares term and a regularization term. This minimization leads to the weak convergence of the solution to the inverse problem, for a specific regularized problem, to the desired solution, for which we have stability and uniqueness proofs. This is demonstrated through numerical examples using the finite element method and the alternating direction method for the semidiscrete problem. We also examine the effects of different regularization methods and the stability of the solution with respect to mesh refinement. This research considers different structural acoustic models, including a focus on the Kirchhoff plate model, and the inverse problem as a boundary identification problem. The numerical examples discussed here also apply to those models. The approach and numerical results can be adapted to other structural acoustic models. The research concludes by outlining potential future work, including the extension to the time-dependent Kirchhoff-Love plate equation, the use of regularization methods, and the application to real-world data. The numerical code used in this research is available online. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model's implications can
be applied to validate the Tsallis distribution and exclude alternative
exponential models, thus ensuring that variations in behavior are indeed reflected
in the standard deviation of impulsivity. Our approach also enables a deeper
understanding of the underlying psychological principles and offers a potential
explanation for the Tsallis distribution's appearance in certain statistical
analyses. Alongside these contributions, we provide a clear and concise explanation
of our model's dynamics and the methods used to analyze it, in addition to a
numerical example that illustrates our approach's applicability to real-data
analysis. We believe that our model's and analysis' features hold value for the
psychological and statistical communities beyond the specific example presented. 
This work is the expanded version of the paper titled ``On the Tsallis delay discounting
model'' that was previously published.

This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Additionally, this approach may provide a richer learning experience compared to traditional, purely analytical explanations. A previous study by other authors, which examined the implications of negative absolute temperature for a two-level system within quantum mechanics, is also discussed. Although their focus was primarily on deriving expression for spontaneous emission, their findings offer additional insights into the concept of negative absolute temperature. A comparison is drawn between their result for the average energy level and the corresponding average occupation number, which can be simplified to provide a more intuitive grasp of the condition necessary for negative absolute temperature. A note is also included on the relationship between negative absolute temperature and the Rayleigh-Jeans paradox, which serves as an interesting historical anecdote. A renowned paper by Einstein, which provided a theoretical explanation for the paradox, is noted for its precursor to his work on photoelectric effect, also earning its own historical significance. The report concludes by highlighting the various meanings that negative absolute temperature can hold, which go beyond the physical context in which it was originally discovered, including a more abstract interpretation that can be applied to the understanding of negative absolute temperature within quantum mechanics, as well as the paradox of Rayleigh-Jeans and the paradox of Boltzmann. The report also proposes a possible alternative for the term negative absolute temperature, suggesting the term "negative energy density" instead, which is supported by graphical and mathematical evidence, specifically in the context of a two-level system, but can be applied to a more general and abstract level. The report further elaborates on this idea by providing a mathematical expression for the condition necessary for negative energy density, which is directly derived from the average occupation number of an energy level, offering a simple and intuitive explanation for this condition. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. The general approach employed here can be applied to other orbital triplets in crystal structures. The associated Python code is publicly available upon request. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. The study also clarifies the relationship between absolute and relative quantum cohomology through the use of rational functions. The findings presented in this paper were previously known in some specialized cases but are now presented as general theoretical principles. The paper in question was initially published in the proceedings of a mathematical conference held at the University of California, Santa Cruz in 2011. The main contributors to this research include R. Castellani, S. Goncharov, R. Davis, H. Konishi, and R. Tsuchiya. The associated mathematical tools draw upon concepts from quantum cohomology, toric geometry, mirror symmetry, and mathematical analysis. The paper in question is divided into five individual sections. The first section provides an introductory overview of the subject matter at hand. The second section explores the relationship between absolute and relative quantum cohomology through the use of rational functions. The third section examines the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. The fourth section investigates the connections between the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. The fifth and final section offers some additional generalizations of the findings presented in the paper. The main contributors to this research, as mentioned earlier, include R. Castellani, S. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our work has significant implications for developing trusted AI models that can detect and correct abnormalities on chest X-rays. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/chexfill. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/ghru/chesterx. Our research was funded by the Amazon Research Scientist Award given to I. Stiels and the Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development Grant under the project AI4Life. Our team is interested in exploring topics related to disease-aware image editing of chest X-rays. Our research was previously published in the Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, the Proceedings of the Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, and the arXiv preprint repository. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application includes a user-friendly
graphical interface and is designed for novice and experienced users alike.
ViDaExpert is specifically tailored for research in archaeology and cultural
studies but is equally applicable to other domains. The application is platform
independent and may be run on Windows, Linux, or Mac operating systems. The
development of ViDaExpert serves as an extension to the former application
ViDa, and the tool, its source code, and documentation are available online at
no cost.
